title: Salt in water
hook: salt you can't find, salty in every sip: the three words 'you are that'
carry: tat tvam asi: you are that

segments.voice: Yesterday: anima, the seed broken open, and nothing at all inside. Your line was the unseen essence holds up the world.
screen: `ANIMA — THE UNSEEN ESSENCE HOLDS UP THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Take a glass of water and a pinch of salt. Drop the salt in, and watch the grains sink, cloud and disappear. Leave it overnight. In the morning, try to pick the salt back out. You can't. It isn't anywhere you can point to. And yet you know it's in there, and you know exactly how to find out. This is Uddalaka's most famous lesson, where his three-word refrain lands with full weight.
screen: `A GLASS OF WATER, A PINCH OF SALT.` → `IN THE MORNING, PICK IT OUT.` → `YOU CAN'T. BUT IT'S THERE.`

segments.voice: Put this salt in water, Uddalaka says, and come to me in the morning. Shvetaketu does. In the morning his father says: bring me the salt you put in last night. He looks, and can't find it; it has dissolved. Sip from this end. How is it? Salty. From the middle? Salty. From the far end? Salty. Then, the father says, you don't see Being here, my dear, but it is truly here. That subtle essence is the self of all this world. That is the truth. That is the self. Tat tvam asi, Shvetaketu. You are that. Those three words are among the most famous in Hindu scripture. Tat, that. Tvam, you. Asi, are. Later teachers counted them among the four great sayings, the mahavakyas, of the Upanishads. The honey and the rivers showed the names dissolving. The seed showed the essence too fine to see. The salt shows it's everywhere at once, in every sip, every drop. And the schools of Vedanta hear the three words differently. Shankara's Advaita hears pure identity: your deepest self and Being are one. Ramanuja hears the self as real and distinct, yet belonging to Brahman, the way a body belongs to its soul. Madhva's Dvaita school reads the same Sanskrit with a different word break, as atat tvam asi: you are not that, not the same as the Lord. All of them taste the same water. And here's why the words matter on an ordinary day: if Being is in every sip, it is in the person across the table too. That's the root of the Hindu habit of seeing the sacred in the one you meet.
screen: `PUT THIS SALT IN WATER.` · `SALTY, SALTY, SALTY.` · `TAT, THAT. TVAM, YOU. ASI, ARE.` · `THREE SCHOOLS HEAR THE WORDS.` · then, large: `TAT TVAM ASI.`

segments.voice: Check for awareness in your hands, your feet, your breath, a sound in the room, the way the son sipped from one end, the middle and the far end. Notice the same plain awareness in every place you check, and rest in that; if you'd like, let tat tvam asi sound once in your mind.
Being, unseen yet truly here, the way dissolved salt can't be picked out, though every sip stays salty.
Your line: tat tvam asi, you are that. Salty in every sip. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Tat tvam asi is one of the four mahavakyas, the great sayings, and in some traditions it is taught to monks at their initiation; each Vedanta school has its own commentary on it.
